questions.question_text: Which line of working establishes that $c^{0}=1$?

options.text: $\frac{c^{9}}{c^{9}}=c^{9-9}=c^{0}$, and an expression divided by itself is $1$

options.why: Uses the multiplication law, which never produces an index of $0$, so it establishes nothing about $c^{0}$.

options.text: $\left(c^{9}\right)^{0}=c^{9\times0}=c^{0}$, and a bracket with index $0$ is empty
options.why: Assumes the result it is meant to prove, and 'an empty bracket' is not a reason a power equals $1$.

options.text: $c^{9}-c^{9}=c^{9-9}=c^{0}$, and a term take away itself is $0$
options.why: Subtracts the terms, which is collecting like terms and gives $0$, not an index law; indices only subtract under division.

questions.solution_text:
$\frac{c^{9}}{c^{9}}$
$=c^{9-9}$
$=c^{0}$
The same expression divided by itself is $1$, so $c^{0}=1$.

questions.solution_text:
$-4y^{0}$
The zero index is written against $y$ only, and the coefficient $-4$ stays.
$=-4\times1$
$=-4$
